chapters.n: The Book of Moses comes from Joseph Smith’s inspired revision of the Bible (JST). This first chapter, revealed in June 1830, has no counterpart in Genesis. It records an experience Moses had on a very high mountain, after the burning bush but before he led Israel out of Egypt.

f.w: caught up into an exceedingly high mountain

f.g: Revealed to Joseph Smith in June 1830 as he began his inspired revision of the Bible.

chapters.n: Moses saw God face to face and talked with him. He could survive God’s presence only because God’s glory rested on him and changed him.

f.w: he saw God face to face
the glory of God was upon Moses

chapters.n: God introduces himself as the Almighty, whose name is “Endless”—without beginning or end.
The first truth God teaches Moses: “Thou art my son.” Before showing him creation, God establishes Moses’ divine identity. His works and words never cease.
No one can see all God’s works without seeing all his glory—and no mortal could see all his glory and remain mortal.
God has a work for Moses. Moses is made in the likeness of the Only Begotten—Jesus Christ—who is and will be the Savior, full of grace and truth. All things are present before God.

f.w: in the similitude of mine Only Begotten
f.g: Similitude = likeness; Moses’ life would foreshadow Christ’s as deliverer and lawgiver.

f.w: all things are present with me

chapters.n: God shows Moses “one thing”—a view of this world—because Moses is in the world.

f.w: this one thing I show unto thee
f.g: A limited view, suited to Moses’ mortal role.

chapters.n: Moses sees the earth from end to end and all its people, past and present, and is filled with wonder.
When God’s presence withdrew, Moses was left alone in his natural state and collapsed to the ground.

f.g: Without God’s glory sustaining him.

chapters.n: After hours of recovery, Moses realizes that “man is nothing” compared to God—something he had never imagined. Yet God has just called him a son. Both truths—our smallness and our divine worth—belong together.
Moses explains he saw God with spiritual, not natural, eyes—he was transfigured, or temporarily changed, so he could endure God’s presence.

f.g: Transfigured = temporarily changed by God’s power to withstand his glory.

chapters.n: Immediately Satan comes, calling Moses “son of man” and demanding worship. Notice Satan’s first move: attacking Moses’ identity as a son of God.

f.w: Moses, son of man, worship me

chapters.n: Moses answers boldly: I am a son of God, like his Only Begotten. Where is your glory that I should worship you? Knowing who he is protects him.

f.w: I am a son of God

f.g: Satan has no true glory to compare with God’s.

chapters.n: Moses points out the contrast: he needed to be transfigured to see God, but he can look at Satan with ordinary eyes.

f.g: In his ordinary, untransfigured state.

chapters.n: Satan’s “glory” is darkness to Moses. He can tell the difference between God and Satan, remembering God’s command to worship God alone.

f.w: I can judge between thee and God
Worship God, for him only shalt thou serve

chapters.n: “Get thee hence, Satan; deceive me not”—Moses rebukes him, again relying on God’s words about his identity.
Moses recalls the burning bush, where God taught him to call upon God in the name of the Only Begotten.

f.w: in the name of mine Only Begotten

chapters.n: Moses refuses to stop praying; he has more to ask. Having felt God’s glory, he can tell God and Satan apart.

f.w: I will not cease to call upon God

chapters.n: Satan throws a tantrum, raging and shouting, “I am the Only Begotten, worship me!”—a blatant lie claiming Christ’s place.

f.g: Spoke or shouted wildly and angrily.

f.w: I am the Only Begotten, worship me

chapters.n: Moses becomes frightened and glimpses “the bitterness of hell.” But by calling on God he receives strength and commands Satan to leave. Fear is real, but prayer brings power.

f.w: calling upon God, he received strength

chapters.n: Satan trembles, the earth shakes, and Moses commands him to depart in the name of the Only Begotten—Christ’s name has power over evil.

f.w: In the name of the Only Begotten, depart hence, Satan

chapters.n: Satan leaves weeping, wailing, and gnashing his teeth, and Moses no longer sees him.

f.g: Grinding teeth in rage or anguish.

chapters.n: Moses recorded this, but because of wickedness it was lost from the Bible—restored now through Joseph Smith.

f.w: it is not had among the children of men

chapters.n: Free of Satan, Moses looks to heaven, filled with the Holy Ghost, who testifies of the Father and the Son.

f.w: the Holy Ghost, which beareth record of the Father and the Son

chapters.n: God’s glory returns. God promises Moses will be stronger than many waters, which will obey his command as if he were God—foreshadowing the parting of the Red Sea.
God promises to be with Moses always, for he will deliver Israel from bondage.
Moses sees the entire earth—every particle—discerning it by the Spirit of God.

f.w: discerning it by the Spirit of God

chapters.n: He also sees every person on the earth, numberless as sand on the seashore.

f.w: numberless as the sand upon the sea shore

chapters.n: He sees many lands, each called earth, with inhabitants—the text may refer to regions of this earth or to other worlds.

f.g: Interpretations vary: lands of this earth or other earths (compare verse 33).

chapters.n: Moses asks two great questions: why are these things so, and by what did you make them?

f.g: Moses asks both purpose (why) and means (how).

chapters.n: Standing in God’s presence, Moses hears that God made all things for his own purpose—and that wisdom remains with God for now.

f.w: For mine own purpose have I made these things

chapters.n: The answer to “by what”: by his word—the Only Begotten Son, full of grace and truth.

f.w: by the word of my power

chapters.n: God has created worlds without number, all through his Son.
The first man is called Adam, which means “many”—he is the father of the human family.

f.g: Hebrew ’adam means “man” or “mankind”; here it signifies all humanity.

chapters.n: God gives an account only of this earth. Many worlds have passed away, many still exist—countless to us, but each known to God.

f.w: all things are numbered unto me

chapters.n: Moses humbly asks to learn about this earth, its people, and the heavens; then he will be content.

f.g: A humble request; Moses accepts God’s limits.

chapters.n: The heavens are many and countless to man, but God numbers them all as his own.
As one earth passes away, another comes; God’s works and words are endless.

f.w: there is no end to my works

chapters.n: Perhaps the best-known verse in the Pearl of Great Price: God’s work and glory is to bring about the immortality and eternal life of his children. Immortality comes to all through Christ’s resurrection; eternal life is living as God lives.

f.g: Living forever with a resurrected body—given to all through Christ.
Life with God and like God—exaltation.

chapters.n: God will now tell Moses about this earth, and Moses must write it down. This introduces the creation account that follows.
People will one day disregard God’s words and remove many from Moses’ book, but God will raise up “another like unto thee” to restore them—understood as Joseph Smith.

f.w: take many of them from the book
I will raise up another like unto thee

chapters.n: A note: the mountain’s name will not be known. These words are now given to Joseph Smith and should be shared only with believers—an instruction for that early time.

f.w: Show them not unto any except them that believe
f.g: An early caution; the Book of Moses was later published in full and canonized in 1880.

chapters.n: This chapter parallels Genesis 1, but God speaks in the first person directly to Moses. A key addition: God created everything through his Only Begotten Son—Jesus Christ was the Creator under the Father.

f.w: by mine Only Begotten I created these things
in the beginning I created the heaven, and the earth

chapters.n: The earth was unformed and empty, and God’s Spirit moved over the waters. Moses adds “I caused darkness to come up”—God is in control even of the darkness.

f.g: Hebrew tohu wa-bohu—formless and empty.

f.w: my Spirit moved upon the face of the water

chapters.n: God speaks, and light appears. Creation happens through his word.
God sees that the light is good and separates it from darkness. Order out of chaos is a theme of creation.

f.w: divided the light from the darkness

chapters.n: God names Day and Night. The creative “day” in Latter-day Saint teaching may be a period of time, not necessarily 24 hours. Abraham’s account calls them “times.”

f.w: the evening and the morning were the first day
by the word of my power

chapters.n: The second day: God makes a “firmament” separating waters below from waters above.

f.g: Hebrew raqia, an expanse—the sky or atmosphere.

chapters.n: God makes the expanse and divides the great waters below from those above—as he spoke, so it happened.

f.w: the waters which were above the firmament
f.g: Ancient language describing clouds and rain from the sky.

chapters.n: God calls the expanse Heaven—the sky. This ends the second day.
The third day: waters gather into one place, and dry land appears.
God names the land Earth and the waters Sea, and sees that it is good.
God commands the earth to produce grasses, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees, each “after his kind”—reproducing its own type.

f.g: Each kind of life reproduces itself; an orderly pattern of creation.

chapters.n: The earth obeys, and plants grow, each producing seed after its kind. God declares it good.

f.w: whose seed should be in itself
f.g: Plants contain the means to reproduce.

chapters.n: The third day ends.
The fourth day: lights in the sky to divide day and night and mark signs, seasons, days, and years.
These lights give light to the earth.

f.w: to give light upon the earth

chapters.n: God makes the sun and moon—here named directly, unlike Genesis—and the stars.

f.w: the greater light was the sun, and the lesser light was the moon
f.g: Genesis avoids naming the sun and moon; Moses names them plainly.

chapters.n: God places them in the sky to light the earth.
The sun rules the day, the moon the night. God sees that everything is good.
The fourth day ends.
The fifth day: the waters teem with life, and birds fill the sky.
God creates great sea creatures, all water life, and every bird after its kind, and sees that it is good.

f.g: Hebrew tanninim—large sea creatures generally.

chapters.n: God blesses them to be fruitful and multiply. Blessing life with increase is a recurring pattern.
The fifth day ends.
The sixth day: land animals—livestock, creeping things, and wild beasts.

f.g: Domestic animals in general, not only cows.

chapters.n: God makes them each after its kind and sees they are good.

f.g: Small creatures that move close to the ground.

chapters.n: God speaks to his Only Begotten: “Let us make man in our image.” Moses clarifies who the “us” is—the Father speaking to the Son. Humans are given stewardship over the earth.

f.w: I, God, said unto mine Only Begotten
f.g: This answers a long-debated question about the plural “us” in Genesis 1:26.

f.w: Let us make man in our image, after our likeness

f.g: Rule or stewardship, implying responsible care.

chapters.n: Man is created in God’s image—in the image of the Only Begotten—male and female. Both men and women bear the divine image.

f.w: male and female created I them

chapters.n: God blesses the man and woman to have children, fill the earth, and care for it.

f.g: Here meaning “fill.”

f.w: Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth

chapters.n: God gives plants and fruit as food for humans. “Meat” in old English simply meant food.

f.g: Food of any kind.

chapters.n: Animals are also given plants to eat. God provides for every living thing.

f.g: Moses adds “clean” to the Genesis wording.

chapters.n: God looks at everything and declares it “very good.” The sixth day ends. Creation, including the human body, is good in God’s eyes.
The heavens and earth and all their “host”—everything in them—are completed.

f.g: All their multitude of inhabitants and elements.

chapters.n: On the seventh day God finished and rested from his work, seeing that it was good.

f.w: I rested on the seventh day

chapters.n: God blessed the seventh day and made it holy—the origin of the Sabbath.

f.g: Made it holy; set it apart.

chapters.n: This is the account (the “generations”) of how the heavens and earth were made.

f.g: History or account of origins (Hebrew toledot).

chapters.n: A distinctive Latter-day Saint teaching: God created all things spiritually before they existed physically on earth. All people were first created in heaven as spirits before there was flesh on earth.

f.w: before they were naturally upon the face of the earth
f.g: There was a spirit creation before the physical one.

chapters.n: A mist rose from the ground to water the land.
God formed man’s body from the earth and breathed life into him; he became a living soul—spirit and body united. Adam was the first flesh on the earth.

f.w: formed man from the dust of the ground

f.g: In Latter-day Saint scripture, the soul is spirit and body together.

f.w: the first flesh upon the earth
f.g: Interpreted variously; often understood as Adam being the first mortal.

chapters.n: God planted a garden eastward in Eden and placed the man there.

f.g: Hebrew, possibly “delight” or “pleasure.”

chapters.n: God made beautiful trees grow, which were also “living souls,” created spiritually first. In the garden’s center were the tree of life and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.

f.w: the tree of knowledge of good and evil

chapters.n: A river flowed out of Eden and divided into four headwaters.

f.g: Four branches or sources.

chapters.n: The first river, Pison, surrounded the land of Havilah, rich in gold.

f.g: Usually spelled Pishon; its location is unknown.

chapters.n: Havilah’s gold was good, and it also had bdellium and onyx.

f.g: Probably an aromatic resin, or possibly a precious stone; uncertain.

chapters.n: The second river, Gihon, surrounded the land of Ethiopia (Hebrew Cush).

f.g: Hebrew Cush; its exact identity in this passage is uncertain.

chapters.n: The third river, Hiddekel (the Tigris), flowed east of Assyria; the fourth was the Euphrates. These names were familiar to Israel and anchor Eden in the known world.

f.g: The Hebrew name for the Tigris River.

chapters.n: God placed Adam in the garden to tend and care for it. Work was part of Eden from the start.

f.w: to dress it, and to keep it
f.g: Dress = cultivate; keep = guard or care for.

chapters.n: Adam may freely eat from every tree.
A crucial addition to Genesis: Adam is forbidden the tree of knowledge, yet “thou mayest choose for thyself.” God gives both a command and agency, and warns of death.

f.w: thou mayest choose for thyself, for it is given unto thee

chapters.n: God tells his Only Begotten it’s not good for man to be alone, so he will make “an help meet” for him—a fitting companion.

f.g: Two words: a “help” that is “meet” (suitable, corresponding). Hebrew ‘ezer kenegdo—a partner equal to and suited for him; ‘ezer is used of God himself.

chapters.n: God brings the animals to Adam to name. They too are living souls, given the breath of life.

f.w: whatsoever Adam called every living creature

chapters.n: Adam names all the animals, but none is a suitable partner for him.

f.w: there was not found an help meet for him

chapters.n: God causes a deep sleep to fall on Adam and takes one of his ribs. Many Latter-day Saint leaders have described the rib account as figurative.

f.g: Often understood symbolically: woman is created from man’s side, as his equal partner.

chapters.n: From the rib God makes the woman and brings her to Adam.
Adam rejoices: “bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.” She is called Woman because she came from man—a wordplay in Hebrew (ishshah/ish).

f.w: bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh

f.g: Hebrew ishshah, sounding like ish, “man.”

chapters.n: This is the foundation of marriage: a man leaves his parents and cleaves to his wife, and they become one. Jesus quoted this verse.

f.g: United completely—physically, emotionally, and spiritually.

chapters.n: They were naked and not ashamed—innocent, with no self-consciousness before the Fall.

Not found in Genesis: God tells Moses that the Satan he cast out is the same being who, before the world, offered to be God’s son and redeem everyone so no soul would be lost—demanding God’s honor in return.

f.w: that one soul shall not be lost
f.g: Satan’s plan sounds generous but would require removing choice.

chapters.n: In contrast, the Beloved Son—chosen from the beginning—said, “Father, thy will be done, and the glory be thine forever.” Christ sought the Father’s glory, not his own.
Satan rebelled, sought to destroy human agency, and wanted God’s own power. By the power of the Only Begotten, God cast him down. This premortal “war in heaven” centered on agency.

f.w: sought to destroy the agency of man

f.g: The God-given ability and freedom to choose and act for oneself.

chapters.n: He became Satan (“adversary”) and the devil, father of lies, who deceives, blinds, and enslaves all who won’t listen to God.

f.g: Hebrew for “adversary” or “accuser.”

chapters.n: Now the story returns to Eden. The serpent was more cunning than any other animal.

f.g: Crafty, cunning.

chapters.n: Moses clarifies that Satan worked through the serpent. He sought to deceive Eve because he did not understand God’s plan; he meant to destroy the world, not realizing the Fall was part of God’s design.

f.w: he knew not the mind of God
f.g: Satan’s ignorance of God’s plan: the Fall he engineered actually opened the way to redemption.
Deceive, trick.

chapters.n: Satan begins with a question twisting God’s words: “Did God really say you can’t eat from every tree?”
Eve answers that they may eat of the trees of the garden.

f.w: We may eat of the fruit of the trees

chapters.n: But not of the tree in the middle—they must not eat or even touch it, or they will die.

f.g: Eve’s report adds “touch,” which is not in God’s recorded command.

chapters.n: The serpent flatly contradicts God: “Ye shall not surely die.” This mixes truth and lie—they would not die immediately, but they would become mortal.
He claims God is withholding something: eating will open their eyes and make them like gods, knowing good and evil. Part of this was true, which made the deception powerful.

f.w: ye shall be as gods, knowing good and evil

chapters.n: Eve saw the fruit was good, beautiful, and desirable for wisdom; she ate and gave some to Adam. Latter-day Saints view their choice as a necessary step that made mortal life and progress possible.

f.w: a tree to be desired to make her wise

chapters.n: Their eyes opened; they realized they were naked and made aprons of fig leaves. Innocence was replaced by awareness.

f.w: they knew that they had been naked

f.g: Coverings tied around the waist.

chapters.n: Hearing God in the garden in the cool of the day, they hid among the trees. Sin brings the impulse to hide from God.

f.w: in the cool of the day
f.g: Literally “the wind of the day,” likely evening breezes.

chapters.n: God calls, “Where goest thou?”—not because he doesn’t know, but to invite Adam to account for himself. (Genesis reads “Where art thou?”)
Adam admits he heard God, was afraid because he was naked, and hid.
God asks who told him he was naked, and whether he ate from the forbidden tree.

f.w: Who told thee thou wast naked?

chapters.n: Adam explains that the woman God gave him—and commanded to stay with him—gave him the fruit. Moses adds that God had commanded Eve to remain with Adam, which helps explain his choice.

f.w: commandest that she should remain with me
f.g: A Moses addition not in Genesis.

chapters.n: God asks Eve what she has done; she answers honestly that the serpent deceived her.
The serpent is cursed to crawl and eat dust—a symbol of humiliation and defeat.

f.w: upon thy belly shalt thou go

chapters.n: God puts hostility between the serpent and the woman, and their offspring. Her “seed” will crush the serpent’s head while the serpent bruises his heel—understood as the first prophecy of Christ’s victory over Satan.

f.w: he shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel
f.g: A heel wound is painful but survivable; a head wound is fatal.
Hostility, deep opposition.

chapters.n: Eve will experience pain and sorrow in childbirth. The phrase about her husband ruling has been explained by Church leaders in terms of loving, presiding partnership rather than domination.

f.w: In sorrow thou shalt bring forth children

f.g: Some modern Church teachings suggest “rule with” as a better sense, stressing equal partnership.

chapters.n: Because Adam ate, the ground is cursed “for thy sake”—for his benefit. Hard work would help him grow.

f.w: cursed shall be the ground for thy sake
f.g: “For thy sake” suggests the hardship is for Adam’s good.

chapters.n: Thorns and thistles will grow; Adam will eat plants of the field.
He will earn bread by sweat until death returns him to the dust from which he came. Mortality and toil are now part of life.

f.w: By the sweat of thy face

chapters.n: Adam names his wife Eve, “mother of all living.” Like Adam, her name represents many.

f.g: Hebrew Chavvah, related to the word for “living.”

chapters.n: God makes garments of skins and clothes them—a tender act of care, and for many readers a symbol of Christ’s covering atonement, since it required a sacrifice.
God tells the Only Begotten that man now knows good and evil, and must not eat from the tree of life and live forever in his sins.

f.w: lest he put forth his hand and partake also of the tree of life

chapters.n: So God sends Adam out of Eden to farm the ground he came from.
God’s words cannot return empty; they must be fulfilled—the warned consequence of death must happen.
God drove them out and placed cherubim and a flaming sword east of Eden to guard the tree of life. This gave Adam and Eve time to repent—a “probationary state.”

f.g: Heavenly guardian beings; also depicted on the ark of the covenant.

f.w: keep the way of the tree of life

chapters.n: A closing note: these are the words God spoke to Moses, now given to Joseph Smith, to be shared only with believers for the time being.
Outside Eden, Adam farmed the land and cared for the animals, earning his bread by hard work as God said. Eve labored alongside him—they were partners from the start.

f.w: Eve, also, his wife, did labor with him
f.g: A Moses addition emphasizing partnership; not in Genesis.

chapters.n: Adam and Eve had sons and daughters, who began to fill the earth. Genesis mentions only Cain, Abel, and Seth at first; Moses shows a larger family existed.

f.g: “Knew” is a biblical idiom for marital intimacy.

f.w: she bare unto him sons and daughters

chapters.n: Their children paired off, spread out, farmed, kept flocks, and had families of their own.

f.g: Pair off as couples.

chapters.n: Adam and Eve prayed together and heard the Lord’s voice from the direction of Eden, though they couldn’t see him—they were now shut out of his presence. Even fallen, they still sought God.

f.w: called upon the name of the Lord

chapters.n: God commanded them to worship him and offer the firstborn of their flocks as sacrifices. Adam obeyed.

f.g: The firstborn animals—the best, given first.

chapters.n: After “many days,” an angel asked Adam why he offered sacrifices. Adam answered, “I know not, save the Lord commanded me”—a model of faithful obedience before full understanding.

f.w: I know not, save the Lord commanded me

chapters.n: The angel explains: the sacrifice is a likeness of the coming sacrifice of the Only Begotten. From the beginning, animal sacrifice pointed to Christ.

f.w: a similitude of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten

chapters.n: Adam is to do everything in the Son’s name and to repent and pray in his name forever.

f.w: in the name of the Son

chapters.n: The Holy Ghost fell on Adam and testified of Christ: as Adam fell, he and all who are willing can be redeemed.

f.w: as thou hast fallen thou mayest be redeemed

f.g: Redemption is offered to all but requires willingness.

chapters.n: Adam, filled with the Spirit, prophesied and blessed God: because of the transgression his eyes are opened, he will have joy in this life, and in the flesh he will see God again.

f.w: in this life I shall have joy
again in the flesh I shall see God

chapters.n: Eve’s great insight: without the transgression they would never have had children, known good and evil, or experienced redemption and eternal life. Latter-day Saints honor Eve’s wisdom and courage.

f.w: Were it not for our transgression we never should have had seed

chapters.n: They praised God and taught everything to their children—the first gospel teachers in a family.

f.w: made all things known unto their sons and their daughters

chapters.n: Satan came claiming to be a son of God too and told them not to believe. Many children chose Satan over God, and people became “carnal, sensual, and devilish”—driven by appetite and evil.

f.w: I am also a son of God
f.g: Satan again attacks identity, as he did with Moses (Moses 1:12-19).

chapters.n: God called people everywhere to repent through the Holy Ghost.

f.w: called upon men by the Holy Ghost everywhere

chapters.n: Those who believed in the Son and repented would be saved; those who didn’t would be condemned—a firm decree.

f.w: as many as believed in the Son

chapters.n: Adam and Eve kept praying. Eve bore Cain and hoped he would follow God, but Cain refused: “Who is the Lord that I should know him?”—echoing Pharaoh’s defiance.

f.w: I have gotten a man from the Lord
Who is the Lord that I should know him?

chapters.n: Then Abel was born, and he obeyed the Lord. Abel kept sheep; Cain farmed.

f.w: Abel hearkened unto the voice of the Lord

chapters.n: Cain loved Satan more than God, and Satan told him to make an offering. His worship was prompted by the wrong source.

f.w: Cain loved Satan more than God

chapters.n: Cain brought produce from his fields as an offering.
Abel brought the firstborn of his flock and the best parts. The Lord accepted Abel’s offering—given in faith as commanded.

f.w: the firstlings of his flock, and of the fat thereof

chapters.n: The Lord did not accept Cain’s offering. Satan was pleased; Cain was furious, and his face fell.

f.g: Very angry.
His expression darkened in anger or sullenness.

chapters.n: God gently asks Cain why he is angry—an invitation to reflect.
If Cain does well, he will be accepted. Otherwise sin waits at the door, and Satan wants him. Cain could still choose.

f.g: Pictured as a crouching animal waiting to pounce.

chapters.n: Cain would become “the father of his lies” and be called Perdition—he too existed before the world. A sobering warning about where his path leads.

f.g: Ruin, loss; a name also given to Satan.

f.w: thou wast also before the world

chapters.n: These evils would be traced back to Cain because he rejected God’s greater counsel—unless he repented. Even here, repentance is offered.
Cain refused to listen to God or to his righteous brother Abel.
Adam and Eve mourned over Cain and their other wayward children—parents’ grief over choices they cannot control.
Cain married one of his nieces, and they loved Satan more than God.

f.g: In the earliest generations, marriage within the family was necessary.

chapters.n: Satan has Cain swear a secret oath on his life, and his followers too, to keep it hidden, especially from Adam. In return Satan promises to deliver Abel into his hands.

f.w: Swear unto me by thy throat
f.g: An oath sealed with a death penalty for breaking it.

chapters.n: Satan swore to do as Cain wished. It was all done in secret—the origin of secret combinations.

f.w: all these things were done in secret

chapters.n: Cain called himself “Mahan,” master of this secret—killing for gain—and gloried in his wickedness.

f.g: The meaning of Mahan is uncertain; it may relate to “mind” or “destroyer.”

f.w: that I may murder and get gain

chapters.n: In the field, Cain spoke with Abel and then rose up and killed him—the first murder.
Cain boasted, “I am free”—now his brother’s flocks were his. Sin promises freedom but brings bondage.

f.g: A tragic irony; Cain becomes a fugitive.

chapters.n: God asks where Abel is. Cain lies and retorts, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” The scriptures answer yes—we are responsible for one another.
Abel’s blood cries out to God from the ground. Injustice does not go unseen.

f.w: The voice of thy brother's blood cries unto me

chapters.n: Cain is cursed from the earth that received Abel’s blood.
The ground will no longer yield its strength to him; he will be a restless wanderer.

f.g: A homeless wanderer.

chapters.n: Cain blames Satan and jealousy over the offering, and complains his punishment is too great—but shows no real repentance.

f.w: my punishment is greater than I can bear

chapters.n: Cain fears being cut off from God and killed by others because of his sins.

f.w: from thy face shall I be hid

chapters.n: God promises sevenfold vengeance on anyone who kills Cain and gives him a mark of protection. Scripture does not say what the mark was; the Church disavows past theories linking it to race.

f.g: Seven times over; complete retribution.

chapters.n: Shut out from God’s presence, Cain lived with his wife and followers in Nod, east of Eden.

f.g: Nod means “wandering.”

chapters.n: Cain had a son named Enoch (not the prophet Enoch) and built a city named after him.
Cain’s line continues: Enoch, Irad, Mahujael, Methusael, and Lamech.

f.g: This Lamech is not Noah’s father, who descended from Seth.

chapters.n: Lamech married two wives, Adah and Zillah—the first recorded plural marriage.
Adah’s sons founded tent-dwelling herding and music. Culture and skill spread even in a wicked line.

f.g: Stringed instruments and pipes or flutes.

chapters.n: Zillah’s son Tubal Cain became the first metalworker; his sister was Naamah.

f.g: A skilled craftsman.

chapters.n: Lamech boasts to his wives that he has killed a man who wounded him.

f.w: I have slain a man to my wounding

chapters.n: If Cain is avenged sevenfold, Lamech claims seventy-sevenfold—escalating vengeance. Jesus later reversed this with “seventy times seven” forgiveness.
Moses explains: Lamech had made Satan’s covenant like Cain and become Master Mahan. Irad, Cain’s grandson, began revealing the secret.
So Lamech killed Irad—not for gain like Cain, but to protect the oath.

f.g: To enforce secrecy.

chapters.n: From Cain’s days there was a secret combination; its works were done in darkness, and members knew each other.
God cursed Lamech and all who covenanted with Satan. Their abominations spread among men.

f.g: God withdrew his presence and help.

chapters.n: Lamech had told his wives the secret, and they rebelled and spread it abroad—women here help expose the evil.

f.g: A Moses addition; the wives refused complicity.

chapters.n: Lamech was despised and cast out, hiding for fear of death.

f.g: Expelled from society.

chapters.n: So works of darkness began to dominate humanity.
God cursed the earth severely and was angry with the wicked.

f.g: Sore = severe.

chapters.n: They refused to listen or believe in the Only Begotten, who would come in “the meridian of time,” prepared before the world.

f.g: The high point or middle of history—the time of Christ’s mortal life.

f.w: prepared from before the foundation of the world

chapters.n: A key Restoration teaching: the gospel of Jesus Christ was preached from the very beginning—by angels, God’s voice, and the Holy Ghost.

f.w: the Gospel began to be preached, from the beginning

chapters.n: All was confirmed to Adam by a holy ordinance, and a decree went out that the gospel would remain in the world until the end.

f.g: Moses 6:64-66 describes Adam’s baptism.

chapters.n: Adam obeyed God and urged his sons to repent. Despite heartbreak over Cain, he kept teaching.

f.w: called upon his sons to repent

chapters.n: Eve bore Seth. Adam praised God for giving another son in place of murdered Abel.

f.g: Hebrew, related to a word meaning “appointed” or “granted.”

chapters.n: God revealed himself to Seth, who offered acceptable sacrifices like Abel. Seth’s son was Enos.
These men began to call on the Lord, and he blessed them.

f.w: call upon the name of the Lord

chapters.n: A “book of remembrance” was kept in Adam’s language, written by inspiration—an early scripture and family record. Latter-day Saints often apply the phrase to family history records.

f.g: The original language given to Adam, described as pure.

chapters.n: Children were taught to read and write in this pure language. Literacy and learning were part of righteous family life from the start.
The priesthood that existed at the beginning will be on earth at the end of the world too.

f.w: this same Priesthood, which was in the beginning

chapters.n: Adam prophesied by the Holy Ghost, and a genealogy was kept. It begins by restating that God made man in his likeness.

f.w: the book of the generations of Adam

chapters.n: God created them male and female “in the image of his own body”—a phrase stronger than Genesis, affirming God has a body. Together they were called Adam.

f.w: In the image of his own body
f.g: A Moses addition; compare D&C 130:22.

chapters.n: At 130, Adam fathered Seth in his own likeness—just as Adam was made in God’s likeness.

f.w: in his own likeness, after his own image

chapters.n: Adam lived 800 more years and had many sons and daughters.
Adam lived 930 years and died—fulfilling the warning that he would die “in the day” he ate, if a day is reckoned as a thousand years.
Seth fathered Enos at 105, prophesied all his life, and taught Enos God’s ways, so Enos also prophesied. Faith passed from parent to child.

f.w: taught his son Enos in the ways of God

chapters.n: Seth lived 807 more years and had many children.
As population grew, Satan gained great power; wars and fratricide arose from secret works seeking power.
Seth died at 912.
Enos fathered Cainan at 90. He led God’s people out of a land called Shulon to a land of promise named after Cainan.

f.g: A place known only from this verse.
An early example of God leading his people to a promised land, a pattern repeated with Abraham, Israel, and Lehi.

chapters.n: Enos lived 815 more years and died at 905.
Cainan fathered Mahalaleel at 70 and died at 910.

f.g: Kenan in many Bible translations; not the same as Canaan.

chapters.n: Mahalaleel fathered Jared at 65 and died at 895.

f.g: Possibly “praise of God.”

chapters.n: Jared fathered Enoch at 162 and taught him all God’s ways—setting the stage for Enoch’s ministry.

f.w: Jared taught Enoch in all the ways of God

chapters.n: This is the genealogy of Adam’s sons. Adam is called “the son of God,” who conversed with God himself.

f.w: Adam, who was the son of God

chapters.n: These patriarchs were preachers of righteousness who called everyone to repent and taught faith.
Jared died at 962.
Enoch fathered Methuselah at 65.
While Enoch traveled among the people, the Spirit of God came down and rested on him. Genesis gives only a few lines on Enoch; Moses 6–7 restore much more.

f.w: the Spirit of God descended out of heaven

chapters.n: A voice calls Enoch “my son” and commands him to preach repentance. The people’s hearts are hard, ears dull, and they cannot see far ahead spiritually.

f.w: their ears are dull of hearing
their eyes cannot see afar off

chapters.n: For generations the people have strayed, denied God, plotted in darkness, devised murder, and ignored Adam’s commandments.

f.w: sought their own counsels in the dark

chapters.n: Their secret oaths have brought death upon them; hell awaits unless they repent.

f.g: Bound by false or wicked oaths; perjured.

chapters.n: This is God’s decree from the beginning, given through Enoch’s fathers and sent forth to the ends of the world.
Enoch bows and asks why God chose him—a young man hated by people and slow of speech. Like Moses and Jeremiah, he feels inadequate.

f.g: A youth. D&C 107:48 says Enoch was ordained by Adam at age 25—young in an age of very long lifespans.

chapters.n: The Lord promises protection and words: open your mouth and it will be filled. God qualifies those he calls.

f.w: Open thy mouth, and it shall be filled

f.g: No one will be able to harm you.

chapters.n: Enoch’s message: choose today to serve the Lord who made you.
The Spirit is on Enoch; mountains will flee and rivers turn at his word. God invites him: “walk with me”—the phrase that defines Enoch in Genesis.

f.w: the mountains shall flee before you

chapters.n: God tells Enoch to anoint his eyes with clay, wash them, and he will see—an act like Jesus healing the blind man.
Enoch saw the spirits God created and things invisible to natural eyes. People said, “The Lord has raised up a seer.”

f.g: One who sees beyond ordinary sight by God’s power.

chapters.n: Enoch preached loudly from hills and high places, testifying against their sins. Everyone was offended.

f.g: Upset, angered, made to stumble.

chapters.n: Curious crowds came, leaving others to guard their tents: “There’s a strange thing in the land—a wild man has come among us!”

f.w: a wild man hath come among us
f.g: Prophets often seemed strange to their audiences, like Elijah or John the Baptist.

chapters.n: No one dared touch him; fear fell on all who heard him, because he walked with God.
A man named Mahijah asked Enoch plainly who he was and where he came from.

f.g: Interestingly, a similar name (Mahaway) appears in the ancient Book of Giants found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, in connection with Enoch.

chapters.n: Enoch explains he came from Cainan, the righteous land of his fathers, where his father taught him God’s ways.
Traveling by the eastern sea, Enoch saw a vision: the heavens opened and the Lord commanded him to speak.
The God who spoke to Enoch is their God too. “Ye are my brethren—why do you deny the God of heaven?”

f.g: Enoch preaches with love, not superiority.

chapters.n: God made the heavens; the earth is his footstool; he placed humanity on it.
Their ancestors have died, but they know about them—even Adam. History testifies of God.

f.w: even the first of all we know, even Adam
f.g: Their records reached back to Adam.

chapters.n: They have a book of remembrance written according to the pattern given by God’s finger, in their own language.
As Enoch spoke God’s words, people trembled and could not stand before him.
“Because that Adam fell, we are”—the Fall made our existence possible, but also brought death and misery.

f.w: Because that Adam fell, we are

chapters.n: Satan tempts people to worship him; they become carnal, sensual, and devilish, shut out from God.
But God revealed that everyone must repent.
God spoke directly to Adam, declaring he made the world and made people before they were in the flesh.

f.w: men before they were in the flesh

chapters.n: The gospel taught to Adam: turn to God, believe, repent, and be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ—the only name for salvation—and receive the Holy Ghost. Christ’s name is given explicitly here, centuries before his birth.

f.g: One of the earliest places in scripture where the Savior is named.

f.w: the only name which shall be given under heaven

chapters.n: Adam asks why repentance and baptism are needed. God answers: I have forgiven you your transgression in Eden.

f.w: I have forgiven thee thy transgression in the Garden of Eden

chapters.n: From this came the teaching that the Son of God atoned for “original guilt”; children don’t bear their parents’ sins. Latter-day Saints reject the idea of inherited guilt.

f.g: The traditional doctrine that all inherit Adam’s guilt; here Christ’s Atonement removes it.

f.w: they are whole from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Children are born into a fallen world, and as they grow, sin begins in their hearts. They taste the bitter so they can value the good—opposition has a purpose.

f.g: Born into a fallen, sinful world—not guilty at birth.

f.w: they taste the bitter, that they may know to prize the good

chapters.n: People can know good from evil, so they are “agents unto themselves”—accountable for their choices. God gives another law.
Teach your children: all must repent, for no unclean thing can dwell with God. In Adam’s language, God’s name is Man of Holiness, and his Son is the Son of Man—Jesus Christ, the righteous Judge.

f.w: Man of Holiness is his name
f.g: So “Son of Man,” Jesus’ favorite self-title, means “Son of the Man of Holiness”—Son of God the Father.

f.w: no unclean thing can dwell there

chapters.n: God commands Adam to teach these things freely to his children.

f.w: teach these things freely unto your children

chapters.n: A beautiful parallel: as we are born physically through water, blood, and spirit, we must be born again through water (baptism), the Spirit, and Christ’s blood, to be sanctified and gain eternal life.

f.w: born again into the kingdom of heaven, of water, and of the Spirit

chapters.n: Water fulfills the commandment, the Spirit justifies (declares us right with God), and the blood sanctifies (makes us holy).

f.g: Declared innocent; brought into right relationship with God.
Made holy and pure.

chapters.n: The Holy Ghost abides in the faithful: the record of heaven, the Comforter, the truth of all things, life-giving power.

f.w: the record of heaven; the Comforter

f.g: Gives life; enlivens.

chapters.n: This is the plan of salvation for everyone, through the blood of the Only Begotten who will come in the meridian of time.
Everything in creation, physical and spiritual, has a likeness that testifies of Christ.

f.w: all things bear record of me

chapters.n: Adam cried to the Lord and was carried by the Spirit into water, laid under, and brought out—baptized by immersion.

f.w: was laid under the water, and was brought forth out of the water

chapters.n: So Adam was baptized, the Spirit descended on him, and he was born of the Spirit and made alive inwardly.
A heavenly voice declares Adam baptized with fire and the Holy Ghost—the witness of Father and Son.

f.w: baptized with fire, and with the Holy Ghost

chapters.n: Adam is made part of the eternal order of priesthood—“after the order of him who was without beginning of days.”

f.w: without beginning of days or end of years

chapters.n: “Thou art one in me, a son of God; and thus may all become my sons.” Adam’s path is open to everyone.

f.w: thus may all become my sons

chapters.n: Enoch keeps preaching, reminding his hearers that Adam taught the gospel from the beginning. Those who believed became “sons of God,” while those who refused now live in dread of coming judgment.

Enoch now tells of a sacred experience: while traveling, he prayed at a place called Mahujah, and a heavenly voice told him to climb Mount Simeon. Like Moses and others, he receives revelation on a mountain.

f.g: A place name known only from this verse; it resembles “Mahujael” in Genesis 4:18 and Moses 5:43.

chapters.n: On the mountain the heavens open and Enoch is “clothed upon with glory” — changed by God’s power so he can endure His presence, much as Moses was transfigured.
Enoch sees the Lord face to face, speaking with Him as naturally as one friend speaks to another. The Lord then promises to show him the history of the world across many generations.
The vision begins with the valley of Shum, home to a large nomadic people living in tents. These ancient peoples are otherwise unknown to us.

f.g: An ancient people and valley named only here and in Moses 7:7; not mentioned in the Bible.

chapters.n: Looking north, Enoch sees another tent-dwelling people called Canaan. This is an antediluvian (pre-Flood) people, not the later Canaanites descended from Noah’s grandson.

f.g: Not to be confused with Canaan son of Ham (Genesis 9:18) or the later land of Canaan; this people lived before the Flood.

chapters.n: At the Lord’s command, Enoch prophesies war: Canaan will destroy the people of Shum, spread through the land, and find it turned barren. Violence was already spreading among Adam’s descendants.

f.g: Lined up and equipped for war.

chapters.n: Enoch foresees the land of Canaan cursed with heat and barrenness, and its people marked and despised. Latter-day Saint leaders have taught that past explanations linking skin color to divine disfavor are wrong and are disavowed by the Church.

f.g: Lack of fruitfulness; the land would no longer support crops.
The meaning here is debated. The Church today teaches that God loves all His children equally and rejects any idea that dark skin signals disfavor (see 2 Nephi 26:33).

chapters.n: Enoch is shown a list of other lands and their inhabitants. Several of these names appear nowhere else in scripture, giving a glimpse of a populated world before the Flood.

f.g: A land named after Enoch himself, or after Cain’s son Enoch whose city bore his name (Moses 5:42).

chapters.n: The Lord sends Enoch to these peoples with a single urgent message: repent, or face a destroying curse. Warning before judgment is God’s consistent pattern.
Enoch is commanded to baptize in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost — showing that the same ordinance and the same Godhead were taught from Adam’s day, long before Christ’s mortal ministry.
Enoch invites every people to repent except Canaan. The narrative now shifts from Enoch’s own words to Moses describing the results of his ministry.

f.g: except for.

chapters.n: Enoch’s faith is so great that when enemies attack, he speaks God’s word and nature itself obeys — the earth shakes, mountains move, rivers change course. The power lay not in Enoch but in the language God gave him.
A new land even rises from the sea, and the frightened enemies flee to it and keep their distance. God physically protects His covenant people.

f.g: kept their distance out of fear.

chapters.n: Even the “giants,” powerful violent men of that era, stay away. Those who fight against God bring a curse upon themselves.
The surrounding world sinks into continual war, yet the Lord comes and dwells among Enoch’s people. Peace in the midst of a violent world is the first mark of Zion.

f.w: the Lord came and dwelt with his people

chapters.n: God’s glory on His people makes other nations stand in awe. The land is blessed, and the people prosper even in the hills and high places.

f.g: Here: reverent awe at God’s evident power over His people.

chapters.n: This is scripture’s classic definition of Zion: a people united in heart and mind, living righteously, with no one left in poverty. It describes a community, not just a place.
Enoch continues teaching and builds a city named the City of Holiness, also called Zion. The ideal society now has a physical home.
Enoch assumes Zion will remain safe forever on earth. The Lord answers that Zion is blessed, but the rest of humanity, by choosing evil, has brought a curse upon itself.

f.g: the rest, the remainder.

chapters.n: In vision Enoch sees all people and watches Zion eventually taken up into heaven. The Lord calls it His own eternal dwelling place.
Enoch sees the remaining descendants of Adam, with Cain’s line separate from them. Readers should be cautious: the Church has disavowed past teachings that tied lineage or skin color to God’s favor.
After Zion’s departure, Enoch is shown all the nations of the earth spread out before him, as the vision moves forward through history.

f.w: all the nations of the earth

chapters.n: Enoch is lifted up spiritually into the presence of the Father and the Son, and from there watches generations pass while Satan’s influence spreads over the whole earth.

f.g: A title of Jesus Christ; Moses 6:57 explains that the Father’s name is Man of Holiness, so the Son is “Son of Man.”

chapters.n: Angels descend, and a voice mourns over the earth’s inhabitants. “Wo” is a lament of grief and warning over people heading toward destruction.

f.g: woe — a cry of grief and warning.

f.w: Wo, wo be unto the inhabitants of the earth

chapters.n: Enoch sees Satan holding a great chain that covers the earth in darkness; Satan laughs while his followers celebrate. The chain pictures how sin binds and blinds humanity.
In contrast, angels testify of the Father and Son, the Holy Ghost falls on many, and these faithful are gathered up into Zion. Even in darkness, God keeps rescuing people.

f.w: caught up by the powers of heaven into Zion

chapters.n: One of scripture’s most moving scenes: the God of heaven looks on the wicked and weeps. Enoch is astonished that heaven itself sheds tears like rain on the mountains.
Enoch asks how a holy, eternal God could weep. His question assumes that a perfect God would be untouched by sorrow — an assumption the Lord is about to correct.

f.w: from all eternity to all eternity

chapters.n: Enoch marvels at God’s vast creations — more than all the particles of millions of earths — yet God is personally present, just, merciful, and kind. Why would such a Being weep?

f.g: The heavens pictured as a tent stretched out by God (Isaiah 40:22).

chapters.n: Enoch adds that God has taken Zion to Himself, and that His throne rests on peace, justice, and truth with endless mercy. With all this joy, “how is it thou canst weep?”

f.w: mercy shall go before thy face

chapters.n: The Lord answers: these people are His own children, whom He made, gave knowledge, and gave agency in Eden. A Father grieves when His children misuse the freedom He gave them.
God had given two great commandments — love one another and choose Him as their Father — but His children are “without affection” and hate their own families. That is why He weeps.
The Lord declares His righteous anger and announces that floods will come. God’s anger here is the response of perfect love to deliberate, destructive evil.

f.g: righteous anger at wrongdoing.

chapters.n: God reveals His names: Man of Holiness, Man of Counsel, Endless and Eternal. These titles teach that God is an exalted, holy Man and the wise Counselor of His children.
Because God holds and sees all His creations, He can say with authority that no other world has seen wickedness as great as among Enoch’s brethren.

f.w: there has not been so great wickedness

chapters.n: The parents who taught them wickedness share responsibility; by following Satan, these people make him their “father.” All heaven weeps because of the suffering they bring on themselves.
Those Enoch is watching will die in the flood, and the Lord has prepared a spirit prison for them. Yet as later verses show, this “prison” is not the end of their story.
Here is the hope: God’s Chosen One — Jesus Christ — has pleaded for them and will suffer for their sins. If they repent when Christ returns to the Father after His Atonement, they can be redeemed.
This, the Lord concludes, is why the heavens weep: His children’s suffering is real, and all His creations mourn with Him.
Seeing what God sees, Enoch is overwhelmed. He weeps, stretches out his arms, and his heart “swelled wide as eternity” — he comes to feel the same love God feels for His children.

f.g: bowels = the inner self, seat of deep feeling; he was moved with compassion.

chapters.n: Enoch sees Noah and his family and learns that Noah’s posterity will be preserved — a “temporal salvation,” meaning physical survival through the Flood.

f.g: rescue of the body and of life on earth, as opposed to spiritual salvation.

chapters.n: Enoch watches Noah build the ark and sees the Lord smile on it and hold it in His hand, while floodwaters swallow the wicked.
Grieved for his brethren, Enoch refuses to be comforted. The Lord gently tells him to lift up his heart and look — there is more to the story than destruction.

f.w: Lift up your heart, and be glad

chapters.n: From Noah, Enoch sees all the earth’s families descend. He asks when the Lord will come and when “the Righteous” (Christ) will shed His blood so that mourners may be made holy and receive eternal life.

f.g: “The Righteous” is a title of Jesus Christ; His shed blood is the source of sanctification.

chapters.n: The Lord answers that Christ will come in the “meridian of time” — the high point or middle of history — during an age of wickedness.

f.g: The noon or high point of history; a Latter-day Saint term for the era of Christ’s mortal ministry (Moses 5:57; D&C 20:26).

chapters.n: Enoch sees Christ’s coming in the flesh and rejoices, declaring that the Lamb was “slain from the foundation of the world” — His sacrifice was planned before creation and worked for believers even before it happened.

f.w: the Lamb is slain from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Enoch hears the earth itself cry out as a weary mother, pained by her children’s wickedness and longing to be cleansed and to rest. Scripture pictures the earth as a living creation that shares in God’s plan.
Moved by the earth’s mourning, Enoch weeps and pleads for God’s compassion on the earth and blessing on Noah’s descendants.

f.g: literally “suffering with” — pity that moves one to help.

chapters.n: Enoch prays in the name of Jesus Christ, the Only Begotten, that Noah’s seed may be preserved and the earth never again flooded. Even before Christ’s birth, prayer was offered in His name.

f.w: in the name of thine Only Begotten
never more be covered by the floods

chapters.n: The Lord “could not withhold” — He made a covenant and oath with Enoch to stop the floods and to call on Noah’s children. This explains the background of the rainbow covenant of Genesis 9.
God decrees that a remnant of Enoch’s seed — through Noah — will always be found among the nations as long as the earth stands.

f.g: a fixed, unchangeable divine promise.

chapters.n: The Lord blesses the one through whose lineage the Messiah will come, and the Messiah Himself speaks: He is the King of Zion and the Rock of Heaven. Those who enter by the gate and climb by Him will never fall.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ — “anointed one”; Greek Christos.

chapters.n: Enoch asks whether the earth will rest when the Son of Man comes in the flesh, and pleads to see these events.
The Lord shows Enoch the Crucifixion: Christ lifted up on the cross “after the manner of men,” dying as mortals die.
At Christ’s death the heavens are veiled, all creation mourns, the earth groans, and rocks split. Faithful saints rise in resurrection and are crowned with glory at the Savior’s right hand.
Spirits in prison who accepted the gospel come forth to God’s right hand, while the unrepentant remain bound until the final judgment. Christ’s redemption reaches even the dead.

f.g: See D&C 138 for Joseph F. Smith’s vision of Christ organizing the preaching of the gospel to the dead.

chapters.n: Enoch, longing for peace, asks again when the earth will finally rest.
Enoch sees Christ ascend to the Father and boldly asks if He will return. He reminds the Lord of His oath and recognizes that his own place before God’s throne comes by grace, not his own merit.
The Lord swears He will come again in the last days, in a time of wickedness, to fulfill His oath concerning Noah’s descendants.

f.g: a solemn oath formula: “as surely as I live.”

f.w: I come in the last days

chapters.n: Before the earth’s rest, there will be darkness, upheaval, and great tribulation; yet the Lord promises to preserve His people.

A key prophecy of the Restoration: righteousness will come down from heaven and truth spring from the earth, testifying of Christ. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in heavenly messengers and the Book of Mormon coming forth from the ground, sweeping the earth to gather God’s elect to a New Jerusalem.

f.w: truth will I send forth out of the earth

chapters.n: Enoch and his city will return to meet the latter-day Zion, and there will be a joyful reunion — embraces and kisses between heaven’s people and earth’s. The two Zions become one.

f.w: thou and all thy city meet them there

chapters.n: That united Zion will be the Lord’s dwelling, and the earth will rest for a thousand years — the Millennium.
Enoch sees Christ come in the last days to dwell on earth in righteousness for a thousand years — the Second Coming and Millennium.

f.w: the coming of the Son of Man

chapters.n: Before then, the wicked will face great tribulation; the sea will be troubled and people’s hearts will fail them for fear of God’s judgments.
The Lord shows Enoch everything to the end of the world, including the redemption of the righteous, and Enoch receives a “fulness of joy.” His sorrow has turned into hope.
Zion lasted 365 years in Enoch’s day. (Genesis 5:23 likewise gives Enoch’s days as 365 years.)
Enoch and his people walked with God until God received Zion into His own presence. The saying “Zion is fled” arose — Zion had been taken from the earth, to return in the last days.
Enoch’s total life span on earth is given as 430 years. Combined with Moses 7:68, this means Zion existed for 365 of those years before being taken up.
Enoch’s son Methuselah was deliberately left on earth when Zion was taken, so God could keep His covenant that Noah would descend from Enoch.

f.g: his physical descendants.

chapters.n: Methuselah prophesies that all the world’s kingdoms will come from him through Noah — and takes pride in it. Even a prophet’s son can be tempted to claim glory that belongs to God.

f.g: took credit or pride for himself rather than giving glory to God.

chapters.n: A severe famine strikes, and many die. This disaster is a sign of the world’s spiritual decline before the Flood.

f.g: sore = severe, grievous.

chapters.n: Methuselah becomes father of Lamech at 187. This genealogy matches Genesis 5 and traces the faithful line from Adam to Noah.

f.g: Not the murderer Lamech of Cain’s line (Moses 5:43-55), but a righteous descendant of Seth.

chapters.n: Methuselah lives another 782 years and has more children. The long lives of these patriarchs gave them centuries to teach the gospel to their descendants.
Methuselah dies at 969 — the longest life span recorded in the Bible, which made his name a byword for old age.
Lamech becomes a father at 182. The sentence continues in the next verse with the son’s name.
Lamech names his son Noah, hoping he will bring comfort and relief from the hard labor of farming cursed ground. The name sounds like the Hebrew words for rest and comfort.

f.g: Hebrew Noaḥ, related to nuaḥ “rest”; the verse plays on naḥam “comfort.”

f.w: the ground which the Lord hath cursed

chapters.n: Lamech lives 595 more years and has other children.
Lamech dies at 777. The faithful line from Adam to Noah is now complete.
Noah’s three sons are born — Japheth first, then Shem forty-two years later by the same mother, and Ham when Noah is 500. Genesis lists only Noah’s age at 500; this verse adds the birth order.
Noah and his sons listen to the Lord and are called “sons of God” — a title for those who make and keep covenants with Him, not heavenly beings.
As the population grows, the “sons of men” — those outside the covenant — marry Noah’s granddaughters simply because they are attractive, without regard to faith.

f.g: In Moses, people who reject God, in contrast to the covenant “sons of God.”

chapters.n: The Lord tells Noah that his granddaughters have “sold themselves” by marrying outside the covenant to men who refuse God. Marrying unbelievers drew Noah’s family toward the world.

f.g: gave themselves away cheaply, trading their covenant heritage for worldly attraction.

chapters.n: Noah becomes a prophet, teaching the same gospel that had been taught from the beginning with Adam.

f.w: even as it was in the beginning

chapters.n: The Lord warns that His Spirit will not always strive with people. He sets a 120-year window — many understand this as time left for repentance before the Flood.

f.g: to struggle with or plead with; the Spirit urges people toward good.

f.w: My Spirit shall not always strive with man

chapters.n: Violent “giants” try to kill Noah, but the Lord protects him and fills him with power. Like Enoch, Noah ministers under divine protection.

f.g: Hebrew nephilim (Genesis 6:4); probably powerful, violent men rather than literal monsters.

chapters.n: The Lord ordains Noah to the priesthood “after his own order” and sends him to preach the gospel, just as Enoch did. Latter-day Saints identify Noah with the angel Gabriel.

f.w: ordained Noah after his own order

chapters.n: Noah calls on everyone to repent, but they refuse to listen.

f.g: did not listen or obey.

chapters.n: The people mock Noah, claiming to be “sons of God” themselves and boasting of normal life — eating, drinking, marrying, and raising mighty children. Jesus later cited these very days as a picture of the world before His return.

f.w: eating and drinking, and marrying and giving in marriage

chapters.n: God sees that wickedness has become universal — people are proud, and every thought in their hearts is evil all the time.

f.w: imagination of the thoughts of his heart

f.g: proud, arrogant.

chapters.n: Despite rejection, Noah keeps preaching and pleading with the people to listen.

f.g: Listen carefully and obey.

chapters.n: Noah’s message is the gospel of Jesus Christ itself: faith, repentance, baptism in Christ’s name, and the gift of the Holy Ghost — the same as later taught in the New Testament and Book of Mormon. Without it, the floods will come.

f.w: be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ

chapters.n: Noah is grieved to the heart that the Lord had ever made mankind, seeing what they have become. Genesis 6:6 says “it repented the Lord”; Joseph Smith’s inspired translation places this regret with Noah.

f.g: Noah regretted or was sorrowful; in Genesis 6:6 the KJV attributes this to the Lord.

chapters.n: The Lord declares He will destroy humanity and animals from the earth, because Noah is grieved and has prayed — and because the people are trying to kill Noah.
Noah finds grace — divine favor — because he is “just” and “perfect in his generation.” Perfect here means complete, whole, upright, not flawless. His sons also walk with God.

f.g: Hebrew tamim — whole, blameless, upright.

chapters.n: The earth is corrupt in God’s sight and full of violence. Violence is singled out as the defining sin of the pre-Flood world.
God looks and confirms the earth’s corruption: every living thing (“all flesh”) has corrupted its way.

f.g: all living beings, especially humankind.

chapters.n: God tells Noah that the end of all flesh has come because of violence, and announces the coming destruction. The story continues in Genesis 6:13 onward.

f.w: The end of all flesh is come before me
